The first-party standard library documents ALL THREE of: a mutual-exclusion primitive, a condition-variable or equivalent blocking-wait/notify primitive, and atomic operations on a machine word.
The first-party standard library provides a message-passing type for transferring values between concurrent workers (channel, queue, mailbox, or equivalent), documented in official documentation.

The language or its first-party standard library provides an asynchronous concurrency model usable without any third-party package (async/await, coroutines, lightweight/green threads, or a first-party event loop), documented in official documentation.

Probe CONC-2 is either rejected at compile time by the toolchain with a diagnostic naming the unsynchronized shared access, OR is reported at run time by a race detector shipped with the toolchain or published by a member of the official_project_set; verified by executing the check on the host.

The first-party standard library provides a structured task-parallelism abstraction above raw threads (task group, thread pool, parallel executor, scoped-thread construct, or parallel collection operation), documented in official documentation.

metrics.scoring_procedure: Count the satisfied indicators among C1-C6 and award the matching level.

levels.name: Parallel, synchronized, asynchronous, race-checked and structured
Sequential
levels.criteria: 0 or 1 of C1-C6 satisfied, which includes any language that cannot achieve parallel speedup and provides no first-party concurrency primitives.

metrics.top_level_evidence_required: To award 100 the evidence record must contain: the CONC-1 probe sources for 1 and 4 workers, all 5 timing runs each, both medians, the computed speedup ratio and the identical numeric results (C1); standard-library documentation URLs with verbatim excerpts for the mutex, the condition variable and the atomics (C2); the channel/queue documentation URL (C3); the asynchronous-model documentation URL (C4); the captured compile-time rejection diagnostic or race-detector report for CONC-2 with the exact command (C5); and the structured-parallelism documentation URL (C6).
metrics.na_policy: Never N/A. A language without first-party concurrency receives the low level, because this metric intentionally tests that capability. C1 is satisfied or not by the measured wall-clock ratio; no language is presumed to pass or fail it, and no runtime property is treated as settling the outcome before measurement. The worker mechanism is whatever CONC-1.worker_model admits, is recorded per language, and a language whose measured 4-worker median does not reach the 1.5x bar fails C1 on that measurement - which is a real result, never an excuse for N/A.

metrics.definition: The number of distinct application domains, from a fixed 12-domain list, for which the language has an obtainable and recently maintained library.
metrics.neutrality_note: The 12 domains are ordinary general-purpose application areas, fixed here before any language is examined. Neutrality is no longer asserted: domain_list_provenance below maps every domain to a category of an external, pre-existing package-index taxonomy that was published long before this benchmark, so the selection is auditable rather than self-certified.

domain_list.domain: Numerical computing / linear algebra (matrix and vector operations)
Graphical user interface or 2D/3D graphics rendering
Compression (for example gzip, zlib or zstd)

metrics.domain_satisfaction_rule: A domain counts as covered for a language only if BOTH hold: (a) a library covering that domain is either part of that language's FIRST-PARTY STANDARD LIBRARY - meaning a module shipped INSIDE the toolchain distribution under test as frozen in environment/environment.json -> toolchains, and nothing else - or is published in that language's qualifying package index as selected by the frozen index_selection_rule in the Library Availability metric (E4); AND (b) that library has a published release, or a documentation version, dated within 24 months before the evidence cutoff 2026-09-17. environment.json's first_party_packages entries are NOT part of any language's standard library for this metric unless they are distributed with the toolchain under test; a separately fetched package published by a language's own project counts, if at all, only through clause (a)'s package-index route, exactly as a third-party package would. This matches the rule the Functionality / Expressiveness metric already applies and is applied identically to all 10 languages. Exactly one library is recorded per covered domain: the first one found by the fixed search procedure. If no qualifying index exists for a language, only standard-library coverage can satisfy a domain, which is a real and reportable property of that language.
metrics.fixed_search_procedure: For each domain, in domain id order: (1) search the language's official standard-library API index (E2) for that domain's frozen query string from frozen_query_list; if a standard-library module shipped inside the toolchain distribution covers the domain, record it and stop. (2) Otherwise query the qualifying package index's own search with the identical frozen query string, using the ordering in frozen_query_list.sort_order, and take the first result whose own description states it covers the domain and whose latest release date is within the 24-month window; record name, version, release date and URL. (3) Otherwise the domain is not covered. The query strings are frozen in this document, not chosen at collection time, and are identical for all 10 languages.
metrics.scoring_procedure: Let N = number of covered domains out of 12. Award the level whose band contains N.
metrics.top_level_evidence_required: To award 100 the evidence record must name, for all 12 domains, the specific standard-library module or package, its version, its release or documentation date inside the 24-month window, and its URL, all collected with the same fixed keyword list used for every language.
metrics.na_policy: Never N/A. A language with no package index and a small standard library receives the low level.

domain_list_provenance.why: Three of the twelve domains (B04 numerical/linear algebra, B05 machine learning, B06 image loading) are precisely the areas where the language under evaluation has first-party coverage, and the 12-domain list was previously asserted neutral rather than derived from anything external. Assertion is not auditable. Each domain is therefore mapped to a category that already existed in a general-purpose package index's own published taxonomy.
domain_list_provenance.source_selection_note: Two indexes from different language ecosystems are cited jointly so that the taxonomy is not taken from any single language's registry. Neither index is a member of any of the 10 languages' official_project_set for the purpose of any indicator; they are used here only as pre-existing external taxonomies.

mapping.B08: PyPI 'Topic :: Multimedia :: Graphics', 'Topic :: Desktop Environment'; crates.io 'gui', 'graphics'

domain_list_provenance.result: All 12 domains map to at least one category that existed in an external taxonomy before this benchmark. No domain was added or removed as a result of the mapping; the list is unchanged and remains frozen.

frozen_query_list._rule: The single most outcome-determining input to this metric, frozen here before any language is searched. Domain coverage for most of the twelve domains depends entirely on which string is typed into each index's search box - 'http' and 'web framework' return different first results and different coverage verdicts - so an unfrozen keyword list made N irreproducible. It was also aggravated by the old collection order, in which the language under evaluation was searched first; global_rules.evidence_collection_order now places it last.
frozen_query_list.query_exactness: The string is typed verbatim, with no added qualifiers, no language name, no quoting, and no substitution of synonyms. The exact query URL issued is recorded per language per domain.
frozen_query_list.sort_order: The index's or API reference's DEFAULT result ordering with no sort parameter changed from its default. The default ordering in force at the accession timestamp is recorded verbatim (for example 'relevance', 'best match') alongside the results.
frozen_query_list.tie_break: If two results are presented at equal rank under the default ordering, take the one whose package or module name sorts first under byte-wise ASCII comparison, and record that a tie occurred together with both candidate names.
frozen_query_list.no_second_query: Exactly one query per domain per language. If the frozen query returns nothing qualifying, the domain is not covered; the scorer may not retry with a different string.
frozen_query_list.symmetry: The same twelve strings are issued for all 10 languages, in the same order, against each language's own standard-library index and its own qualifying package index. No string names a language, a library, or a feature that any single language has.

metrics.definition: The presence of six developer tools admissible for the language under global_rules.tool_admissibility_test, and how many of them are present and runnable on the frozen measurement host.

indicators.text: An admissible build driver: a command that builds a multi-file project without hand-written per-file compiler invocations.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the tool satisfied.

indicators.text: An admissible code formatter that rewrites source into a canonical form.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the tool satisfied.

indicators.text: An admissible linter or static analyzer that reports issues beyond the compiler's or interpreter's default error set.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the tool satisfied.

indicators.text: An admissible test runner command that discovers and executes tests.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the tool satisfied.

indicators.text: An admissible API documentation generator that produces documentation from source declarations and doc comments.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the tool satisfied.

indicators.text: An admissible package or dependency manager command.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the tool satisfied.

metrics.host_presence_check: Independently of satisfaction, for each satisfied indicator the scorer records the tool's state from global_rules.tool_availability_states, executing its documented version command on the frozen host (E1) and capturing the output where it is present. H = the number of satisfied indicators whose tool is in state S5 (present and executed) OR state S2 (the language's official documentation states it ships with the official distribution, but it is absent from this host's repackaged install). Tools in states S1, S3 and S4 do not count toward H, and every S2, S3 and S4 case is published in the host-limited indicators table. H is scored on the reason rather than on bare execution because this host's ten toolchains were provisioned by different routes - Homebrew repackages, Xcode bundles, and one toolchain built locally from source - and a repackaging accident is not a language property.
metrics.scoring_procedure: Let T = number of satisfied indicators among T1-T6 and H = number of those tools that were successfully executed on the frozen host. Award the highest level whose criteria are met, testing from 100 downward.
metrics.top_level_evidence_required: To award 100 the evidence record must contain, for all six tools, the URL and verbatim excerpt establishing the admissibility clause (a, b or c) with the publisher named, plus, for at least four of them, either the exact version command executed on the host with its captured output and exit status (state S5) or the official documentation statement that the tool ships with the official distribution together with the host evidence of its absence (state S2).
metrics.na_policy: Never N/A. A language for which fewer than two admissible tools exist receives 0 on this metric.
metrics.admissibility: T1-T6 count any tool admissible under global_rules.tool_admissibility_test: published by a member of the official_project_set (clause a), OR named by the language's official documentation as a/the way to do that task (clause b), OR invoked by the official implementation repository's own CI configuration (clause c). The satisfied clause is recorded per tool. Restricting this metric to clause (a) would have erased the third-party build, test, format and package tooling that constitutes an established language's real ecosystem advantage, which spec section 7 forbids discounting.

metrics.definition: The size of the language's obtainable third-party library population, measured as the total published package count of the single qualifying package index selected for that language by the frozen index_selection_rule.

index_selection_rule.qualification: A package index QUALIFIES for a language if it distributes libraries for that language AND satisfies at least one of: (i) it is referenced by a member of the language's official_project_set in official documentation; (ii) it is the default remote of a package manager that the language's official documentation names; (iii) it is published or maintained by a maintainer of an implementation listed in that language's major_implementations (official_project_table).
index_selection_rule.selection: Among qualifying indexes, select the one with the LARGEST total published package count as self-published by that index. Record why it qualified, which clause it satisfied, and the counts of every other qualifying index considered.
index_selection_rule.count_source: The index's own published total, taken from its front page, its statistics page, or its documented public API. Record the figure verbatim with its URL and accession timestamp. Do not estimate, extrapolate, or sum across indexes.
index_selection_rule.no_qualifying_index: If no index qualifies for a language at the evidence cutoff, the recorded count is 0 and the language receives the level for count 0. This is a real property of the language's present ecosystem and is not N/A.
index_selection_rule.fairness_note: Clause (iii) exists so that a language governed by a standards body rather than by a single vendor is not scored as having no libraries merely because its standards body does not operate a registry. It is written language-neutrally and may be used by any of the 10 languages. The implementations it refers to are frozen per language in official_project_table.major_implementations, so the clause no longer turns on an undefined judgement about which implementations are 'major'.

metrics.scoring_procedure: Let C = the selected index's published package count (0 if no index qualifies). Award the level whose band contains C.

levels.name: Very large library population
levels.criteria: C >= 100000 published packages in the selected qualifying index.

levels.name: No qualifying index
levels.criteria: C = 0, meaning no index satisfying the qualification clauses exists for the language at the evidence cutoff, or the qualifying index publishes no packages.

metrics.top_level_evidence_required: To award 100 the evidence record must name the selected index, state which qualification clause it satisfied with the supporting URL and verbatim excerpt, give the index's own published package-count figure verbatim with its URL and accession timestamp, and list every other qualifying index considered with its count, showing the selected one is the largest.
metrics.na_policy: Never N/A. Absence of a package index is scored 0.

metrics.definition: The capability of the language's package manager: existence, transitive resolution, version pinning, version-constraint expression, offline/cached operation, and integrity verification.
metrics.manager_selection_rule: The package manager evaluated is the one shipped with the language's official toolchain distribution if such a manager exists; otherwise the package manager whose default remote is the index selected by the Library Availability index_selection_rule. Record which manager was evaluated and why. If neither exists, all indicators M1-M6 are unsatisfied.

indicators.text: A package manager for the language exists under the manager_selection_rule and its documentation is published by a member of the official_project_set or by the manager's own maintainers.
The manager resolves transitive dependencies automatically from a declared direct-dependency manifest, as stated in its documentation.
The manager produces a lockfile or an equivalent artifact that records the exact resolved version of every direct and transitive dependency for reproducible rebuilds, as stated in its documentation.
The manifest format supports version constraints or ranges (not only exact pins), with the constraint syntax documented.
The manager supports building from a local cache, a vendored copy, or a documented offline mode after an initial fetch, as stated in its documentation.
The manager verifies the integrity of fetched packages using checksums, hashes or signatures, as stated in its documentation.

metrics.host_presence_check: Record the selected manager's state from global_rules.tool_availability_states, executing its documented version command on this host (E1) and capturing the output where it is present. INSTALLED is true if the manager is in state S5 (present and executed) or state S2 (official documentation states it ships with the official toolchain distribution but it is absent from this host's repackaged install), and false otherwise. Every S2, S3 and S4 case is published in the host-limited indicators table.
metrics.scoring_procedure: Let M = number of satisfied indicators among M1-M6. Award the highest level whose criteria are met, testing from 100 downward.

levels.name: Complete and toolchain-integrated
levels.criteria: M = 6 AND INSTALLED is true (per host_presence_check: the manager is in state S5 or state S2).

levels.name: Complete or near-complete
levels.criteria: M = 6 AND INSTALLED is false, OR M = 5.

levels.name: None or manual
levels.criteria: M <= 1, which includes any language for which no package manager exists under the manager_selection_rule.

metrics.top_level_evidence_required: To award 100 the evidence record must contain six documentation URLs with verbatim excerpts, one per indicator, plus either the manager's version command executed on the host with its captured output and exit status, or the official documentation statement that it ships with the official toolchain distribution together with the host evidence of its absence and the recorded state S2.
metrics.na_policy: Never N/A. A language with no package manager receives 0.

metrics.definition: The existence and feature depth of editor integration for the language that is admissible under global_rules.tool_admissibility_test (I1, I4, I6), together with a first-party syntax grammar (I5).
metrics.admissibility: I1, I4 and I6, and the selection of the language server that I2 and I3 are scored against, count any tool admissible under global_rules.tool_admissibility_test: published by a member of the official_project_set (clause a), OR named by the language's official documentation as a/the way to do that task (clause b), OR invoked by the official implementation repository's own CI configuration (clause c). The satisfied clause is recorded per tool. Restricting these indicators to clause (a) would have excluded jdt.ls for Java, the clangd-based and MSVC-based integrations for C++ and the Pyright/Pylance-class servers for Python, which is the third-party editor ecosystem spec section 7 forbids discounting as an incumbency effect. I5 is deliberately NOT widened: it asks specifically whether the language's OWN project publishes a grammar, and it keeps the official_project_set test for all 10 languages.
metrics.language_server_selection_rule: I2 and I3 are scored against the BEST language server admissible under global_rules.tool_admissibility_test for that language - 'best' meaning, mechanically, the admissible server whose published feature list covers the most of the six capabilities named in I2 and I3, with ties broken by the earlier admissibility clause (a before b before c) and then by byte-wise ASCII order of the server's name. I2 and I3 are therefore NOT tied to whichever server I1 was recorded against, and a language does not lose I2/I3 merely because its official project publishes no server of its own. If NO language server is admissible for a language under any of the three clauses, I1, I2 and I3 are ALL unsatisfied for that language. The selected server, its publisher, its admissibility clause and its feature-list URL are recorded.

indicators.text: A Language Server Protocol implementation (or an equivalent documented editor-integration server) for the language exists and is admissible under global_rules.tool_admissibility_test.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the server satisfied.

indicators.text: The official documentation or published feature list of the language server selected by language_server_selection_rule states that it provides ALL THREE of: diagnostics, code completion, and go-to-definition. If no admissible server exists, I2 is unsatisfied.

That same selected server's documentation or published feature list additionally states that it provides ALL THREE of: hover type/signature information, find-references, and rename or another automated refactoring. If no admissible server exists, I3 is unsatisfied.

An editor extension or plugin for the language is published in a widely used editor's official extension marketplace or plugin repository, and that extension is admissible under global_rules.tool_admissibility_test.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the extension satisfied.

indicators.text: A first-party syntax grammar or editor mode for the language (TextMate grammar, tree-sitter grammar, or editor major mode) is published in an official repository of the official_project_set. This indicator keeps the official_project_set test and is not widened by the admissibility test.
A dedicated IDE for the language, or an IDE plugin, admissible under global_rules.tool_admissibility_test, has a published release dated within 24 months before the evidence cutoff.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the IDE or plugin satisfied.

metrics.scoring_procedure: Count the satisfied indicators among I1-I6 and award the matching level.

levels.name: None
levels.criteria: 0 or 1 of I1-I6 satisfied, which includes a language for which no admissible language server and no admissible editor integration exists.

metrics.top_level_evidence_required: To award 100 the evidence record must contain the language server's repository or documentation URL, its publisher and its admissibility clause (I1), the selected server under language_server_selection_rule together with every admissible server considered, and verbatim feature-list excerpts covering all six named capabilities (I2, I3), the marketplace listing URL with its publisher field and admissibility clause (I4), the official grammar repository URL and file path (I5), and the IDE or IDE-plugin release page URL, its admissibility clause and a release date inside the 24-month window (I6).
metrics.na_policy: Never N/A. A language with no admissible editor integration receives 0.

metrics.definition: The ability to produce debug information, to debug at source level with language-level value rendering, to profile CPU and memory, and to debug from an editor through a documented protocol integration.

indicators.text: The toolchain emits standard source-level debug information (DWARF, PDB, source maps, or an equivalent documented format) through a documented flag or mode; verified by building DBG-1 on the host with that flag and confirming the debug information exists in the produced artifact or in a companion file.

A source-level debugger supporting the language is either shipped with the toolchain or named in the language's official documentation, and on this host it can set a breakpoint on a source line of DBG-1, stop there, and print the value of a local variable.

In that debugger session, the named fields of the user-defined aggregate and the elements of the standard-library dynamic array in DBG-1 are displayed as language-level values with their field names/elements, not only as raw addresses or bytes.

A CPU profiler for the language is shipped with the toolchain or named in the language's official documentation, and on this host it produces a profile of DBG-1 attributing cost to named functions of the program.
A memory, allocation or heap analysis tool for the language is shipped with the toolchain or named in the language's official documentation.

A Debug Adapter Protocol integration, or an equivalent documented editor-debugging integration, exists for the language and is published by a member of the official_project_set or by a maintainer of an implementation listed in that language's major_implementations (official_project_table).

metrics.scoring_procedure: Count the satisfied indicators among Q1-Q6 and award the matching level.

levels.name: None
levels.criteria: 0 or 1 of Q1-Q6 satisfied, which includes a language with no source-level debugger and no profiler.

metrics.top_level_evidence_required: To award 100 the evidence record must contain: the debug-build command and the command output identifying the debug information (Q1); the full debugger transcript showing the breakpoint hit, the source line, and the printed local (Q2); the transcript lines showing the aggregate's named fields and the array's elements (Q3); the profiler command and the captured per-function profile output (Q4); the documentation URL for the memory/heap tool (Q5); and the DAP or editor-debug integration repository/marketplace URL with its publisher (Q6).
metrics.na_policy: Never N/A. A language with no debugger and no profiler receives 0, because this metric intentionally tests that capability.

metrics.definition: The degree to which building and testing a multi-module project, including coverage and machine-readable results usable by continuous integration, is supported by tooling admissible for the language under global_rules.tool_admissibility_test.
metrics.admissibility: V1-V5 count any tool admissible under global_rules.tool_admissibility_test: published by a member of the official_project_set (clause a), OR named by the language's official documentation as a/the way to do that task (clause b), OR invoked by the official implementation repository's own CI configuration (clause c). The satisfied clause is recorded per tool. The indicator texts below say 'admissible' rather than 'first-party' for exactly this reason: restricting them to clause (a) would have excluded Maven, Gradle and JUnit for Java, CMake, CTest and googletest for C++, Gradle for Kotlin and pytest/pip for Python, which is the third-party build and test ecosystem that spec section 7 forbids discounting as an incumbency effect. V6 is a documentation indicator and is unchanged.
metrics.probe_set: TEST (probes TEST-1 and TEST-2, frozen in frozen_probe_sets)

indicators.text: A build system or build driver admissible under global_rules.tool_admissibility_test builds probe TEST-2 (at least two source modules plus a test module) from a declarative manifest or project-definition file belonging to the project, without hand-written per-file compiler invocations; verified on the host. BOTH conjuncts are required (global_rules.indicator_model.no_partial_credit): the driver must consume a manifest or project-definition file, AND no per-file compiler invocation may be hand-written. Naming a single entry source file that imports the project's other modules is NOT a manifest or project definition and does not satisfy V1. The only exception is the general rule in rubric_verification_recipes._general_rules.languages_with_no_separate_build_step, which is stated in language-neutral terms, is available to any of the 10 languages whose official toolchain performs no separate compilation step at all, and is not available to any language that does compile.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the tool satisfied.

indicators.text: A test construct or test framework admissible under global_rules.tool_admissibility_test is used to express probe TEST-1. Admissibility is the three-clause test; the framework need not ship with the toolchain distribution. (The narrower 'shipped with the toolchain distribution' test survives separately as capability X22 of the Functionality / Expressiveness metric; see that metric's overlap_declaration.)
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the tool satisfied.

indicators.text: An admissible test runner command discovers and runs probe TEST-1, reports the pass and fail counts (2 pass, 1 fail), and exits with a non-zero status because of the failing test; verified on the host.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the tool satisfied.

indicators.text: Code-coverage instrumentation from an admissible tool is available through a documented flag or subcommand and produces a coverage report for probe TEST-1 on the host.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the tool satisfied.

indicators.text: The admissible test runner can emit machine-readable results (JSON, JUnit XML, TAP, or an equivalent documented format) through a documented flag; verified on the host by producing the file and parsing it successfully. Machine-readable DIAGNOSTIC output is not test-result output and may not be counted for V5 for any language.
indicators.admissibility: global_rules.tool_admissibility_test; record which clause (a/b/c) the tool satisfied.

indicators.text: Official documentation describes continuous-integration usage of the toolchain: documented exit-status semantics for failed builds/tests plus a documented non-interactive/CI mode, or an officially published CI action, workflow or container image.

metrics.scoring_procedure: Count the satisfied indicators among V1-V6 and award the matching level.

levels.name: Full admissible build, test, coverage and CI integration
None
levels.criteria: 0 or 1 of V1-V6 satisfied, which includes a language with no admissible build driver and no admissible test facility.

metrics.top_level_evidence_required: To award 100 the evidence record must contain the manifest or project-definition file and the build command for TEST-2 with its successful exit status (V1); the TEST-1 sources showing the admissible test construct, its admissibility clause and its documentation URL (V2); the runner command, its captured 2-pass/1-fail output and its non-zero exit status (V3); the coverage command and the produced report (V4); the machine-readable output command, the produced file and proof it parsed (V5); and the CI documentation URL with a verbatim excerpt (V6).
metrics.na_policy: Never N/A. A language without admissible build or test tooling receives the low level.

metrics.definition: The amount of named, citable, publicly retrievable evidence that the language is used in production outside its own maintainers, plus the existence of a formal steward with a published support policy.
metrics.anti_fabrication_rule: Every organization, product, figure and survey counted here MUST be backed by a retrievable URL, a publication date, and a verbatim excerpt of at most 15 words recorded in the evidence record. Counts asserted from memory, from model prior knowledge, or from undated or unattributed sources are prohibited and must be recorded as unverified and therefore unsatisfied. The scorer may not infer adoption from a language's popularity.

indicators.text: At least 1 named organization other than the language's own maintainers has published a retrievable, dated statement that it uses the language in production, or appears by name on an official case-study/user page published by the language's own project.
At least 5 such distinct named organizations, each with its own distinct citation.
At least 20 such distinct named organizations, each with its own distinct citation, or an official case-study/user page published by the language's own project that names at least 20 organizations.
The language has a formal governance body, foundation, or named corporate steward that publishes an official governance document and an official release or support policy.
At least one end-user-distributed product, service, or infrastructure component states in its own official documentation or official repository that it is implemented in the language.

The language appears with a non-zero reported share or rank in at least one publicly retrievable, methodologically documented developer-population survey or language index published within 24 months before the evidence cutoff; the source, the methodology statement and the figure are recorded verbatim.

metrics.scoring_procedure: Count the satisfied indicators among A1-A6 and award the matching level.

levels.name: Broad documented production use with formal stewardship

metrics.top_level_evidence_required: To award 100 the evidence record must list at least 20 distinct named organizations with 20 distinct dated URLs and verbatim excerpts, the governance document URL and the release/support policy URL, the shipped product with its official statement of implementation language, and the survey/index source with its methodology statement and the language's figure quoted verbatim. A shortfall in any one of these forbids 100 regardless of how well known the language is.
metrics.na_policy: Never N/A. A language with no retrievable third-party production evidence receives 0. This is the expected and correct outcome for a language with no external users at the evidence cutoff, and no allowance is made for the language's age.

metrics.definition: The completeness of first-party documentation (language reference, standard-library API reference, tutorial, toolchain/CLI reference) and the existence of demonstrably active public community and issue-tracking channels.

indicators.text: A first-party language reference or specification document, describing the language's syntax and semantics, is published at the official documentation root.
A first-party standard-library API reference is published, covering the standard library at a stated version, with per-item entries (types/functions/modules).
A first-party tutorial or getting-started guide that walks a new user from installation to a running program is published.

First-party toolchain/CLI reference documentation exists for the commands used in the frozen recipes: either published command reference pages/man pages, or built-in --help output that enumerates the subcommands and options; verified on the host for the installed toolchain.

An official public community channel (forum, mailing list, chat server, or discussion board) is designated on the official site, and it contains at least one publicly visible message posted within 90 days before the evidence cutoff.

A public issue tracker for the language implementation is publicly visible and contains at least one issue opened within 90 days before the evidence cutoff by an account that is not a listed maintainer of the project.

metrics.scoring_procedure: Count the satisfied indicators among N1-N6 and award the matching level.

levels.name: Complete documentation with active public community

metrics.top_level_evidence_required: To award 100 the evidence record must contain four documentation URLs with verbatim excerpts (N1-N3 plus the command reference for N4, or the captured --help output for N4), the community channel URL with the date of a message inside the 90-day window, and the issue-tracker URL with the issue number, its opening date inside the 90-day window, and the reporter's non-maintainer status.
metrics.na_policy: Never N/A. Sparse documentation or an inactive community receives the low level.

metrics.definition: The published release history, versioning status, age, compatibility policy, release cadence and maintenance policy of the exact toolchain implementation under test.
metrics.scope_rule: All indicators are evaluated against the toolchain implementation named in environment/environment.json -> toolchains for that language, and its official release history in the official_implementation_repository or official download archive. Where a language has both a standard and an implementation, the release history is the implementation's; the standard may only be used for Y4.

indicators.text: The toolchain has a published release history containing at least 10 distinct released versions with retrievable release notes, tags, or dated download artifacts.

The version under test is at or above 1.0 under the project's own published versioning scheme, or the project publishes an explicit statement that the current release line is stable for production use.
At least 10 years elapsed between the first publicly released version of the toolchain and the evidence cutoff 2026-09-17, evidenced by the dated first release.

An official, documented stability or compatibility policy exists: a backward-compatibility guarantee, a documented deprecation policy, or a published language-version/edition/standard mechanism that defines how existing source keeps compiling across releases.
At least 2 releases of the toolchain were published in the 12 months before the evidence cutoff, or the project publishes a documented regular release schedule and met it in that period.

A documented maintenance policy names which released versions receive continued bug-fix or security maintenance and for how long (long-term support designation, security-fix window, or supported-versions table).

age_floor.rule: AGE FLOOR, applied BEFORE the indicator count: if fewer than 3 years elapsed between the toolchain's first public release and the evidence cutoff 2026-09-17, the metric scores 0 regardless of how many of Y1-Y6 are satisfied. If at least 3 years elapsed, the level is determined by the indicator count alone.
age_floor.why: The former Y3 was a binary 3-year test and the former Y1 asked for only 3 released versions, so a weeks-old toolchain could reach 'Developing' (40) on a metric named Release Maturity while a thirty-year-old one reached 100. Y1 now asks for 10 released versions and Y3 for 10 years elapsed, and the discarded 3-year threshold is retained here as the floor for scoring anything above 0 rather than being deleted.
age_floor.symmetry: The floor is a dated fact about a toolchain's first public release and is tested identically for all 10 languages. Any of the 10 would score 0 if its toolchain were less than 3 years old; none is named in the rule. It is a maturity floor, not a young-language allowance, and it moves scores only downward.
age_floor.evidence: The dated first public release is recorded for every language, with URL and accession timestamp, whether or not the floor binds.

metrics.scoring_procedure: First apply the age_floor. If it binds, the score is 0 and no further test is made. Otherwise count the satisfied indicators among Y1-Y6 and award the matching level.

levels.name: Mature, stable, maintained and scheduled
levels.criteria: Age floor passed AND all 6 indicators satisfied.

levels.name: Strong
levels.criteria: Age floor passed AND exactly 5 of Y1-Y6 satisfied.

levels.name: Established
levels.criteria: Age floor passed AND exactly 4 of Y1-Y6 satisfied.

levels.name: Developing
levels.criteria: Age floor passed AND exactly 3 of Y1-Y6 satisfied.

levels.name: Early
levels.criteria: Age floor passed AND exactly 2 of Y1-Y6 satisfied.

levels.name: Pre-release
levels.criteria: The age floor binds (fewer than 3 years since first public release), OR 0 or 1 of Y1-Y6 satisfied. This includes a toolchain below 1.0 with fewer than ten published releases, less than ten years of history, and no published compatibility or maintenance policy.

metrics.exhaustiveness_verification: The floor partitions the languages into two groups. Within the group that passes it, the counts 0-6 map to exactly one level each (6->100, 5->80, 4->60, 3->40, 2->20, 0 or 1->0), so the bands still partition 0-6 satisfied indicators. Within the group that fails it, the score is 0 for every count. No combination matches two levels and none matches zero levels.
metrics.top_level_evidence_required: To award 100 the evidence record must contain the dated first public release passing the age floor and proving at least 10 years of history (age_floor, Y3), the release-history URL with at least 10 version identifiers and dates (Y1), the version string of the toolchain under test with the project's versioning-scheme statement or stability statement (Y2), the compatibility/deprecation/edition policy URL with a verbatim excerpt (Y4), the identifiers and dates of at least 2 releases inside the 12-month window or the schedule document plus the releases meeting it (Y5), and the maintenance/LTS policy URL with the named supported versions and windows (Y6).
metrics.na_policy: Never N/A. A pre-1.0 toolchain with a short history receives the low level, and a toolchain less than 3 years old receives 0 under the age floor. No age adjustment or young-language allowance is applied in the other direction.

_preamble.purpose: Per-finding record of the adversarial audit remediation applied to this document. Each entry gives the finding's severity, the defect in one line, what was changed, and - for every Quidra-bias finding - the DIRECTION the correction is expected to move Quidra's score.
_preamble.no_results_observed: NO SCORE HAS BEEN COMPUTED from this document or from any sibling methodology document. No language has been measured under any rubric here. Every threshold, band, indicator, recipe, table and query string, including every one introduced or changed by this remediation, was fixed before any measurement. This is pre-registration, not post-result formula selection, and it is therefore permitted by spec 25.4 and not a violation of spec 32's ban on modifying weights after seeing results.
_preamble.correction_direction_rule: Every finding was applied in the direction the auditor specified. No finding was resolved by weakening it, by declaring it out of scope, by adding a caveat while keeping the biased rule, or by adding a compensating bias in the other direction.
_preamble.symmetry_test_applied: Every change was checked against the question 'would this look equally reasonable if Quidra were replaced by Zig, or by Python?'. No rule in this document now turns on a property that only one of the ten languages happens to have or lack.
_preamble.net_direction: LOWER. The corrections remove a first-party-publisher gate that had handed a monolithic young toolchain parity with established ecosystems on three metrics, remove a Quidra-specific exemption from a build indicator, remove a Quidra-only second diagnostic command, and raise the release-maturity bar. Nothing here was changed in a direction that favours Quidra.

findings.defect: A 'published by a member of official_project_set' gate on Tooling (T1-T6), Build / Test Integration (V1-V5) and IDE / Editor Support (I1, I4, I6) erased the third-party ecosystem that constitutes incumbency - Maven, Gradle, JUnit, CMake, googletest, npm, pytest - which spec section 7 forbids discounting as an 'incumbency effect'.
findings.change: Added global_rules.tool_admissibility_test: a frozen, language-neutral three-clause test (a: published by the official_project_set; b: named by the language's official documentation as a/the way to perform that task; c: invoked by the official implementation repository's own CI configuration), applied identically to all 10 languages, with the satisfied clause recorded per tool. T1-T6, V1-V5 and I1/I4/I6 now read 'admissible' rather than 'first-party'; their metric definitions, level names, na_policy lines and top_level_evidence_required lines were updated to match, so the rule is no longer stated one way in a metric definition and another way in its indicators. I5 deliberately keeps the official_project_set test, because it asks specifically whether the language's own project publishes a grammar. Added IDE / Editor Support language_server_selection_rule, which decouples I2 and I3 from I1 by scoring them against the best admissible language server (mechanically: most of the six named capabilities covered, ties broken by earlier admissibility clause then byte-wise name order), and states explicitly that if no admissible server exists, I1, I2 and I3 are ALL unsatisfied.
findings.quidra_score_direction: LOWER. Quidra's own indicators are untouched, but Java, C++, Python, Kotlin and TypeScript can now count the build, test, format, package and editor tooling they actually have, so Quidra's relative position on three of the ten Ecosystem / Production Maturity metrics falls.

findings.defect: Dependency Simplicity's level set was not exhaustive: the case D_total = 0 AND offline_build FAILS matched no level, leaving a free judgement call at scoring time.
findings.change: Level 20's criteria now read '11 <= D_total <= 50, OR (1 <= D_total <= 50 AND pinning is not available), OR (1 <= D_total <= 50 AND offline_build fails), OR (D_total = 0 AND offline_build fails)'. Added an exhaustiveness_verification block enumerating every (D_total band x pinning x offline_build x install_units) combination and showing each matches exactly one level.
findings.quidra_score_direction: UNCHANGED for Quidra specifically; the new clause can only lower a score, and it applies to whichever languages fail the cache-emptied offline build, which is not known and was not looked at.

findings.defect: The commands needed to verify V1-V5, DEP-1, FFI-2 to FFI-4, CONC-1, DBG-1 and PORT-1 were frozen nowhere, so a literal reading of indicator_model.unverifiable_rule zeroed Build / Test Integration for all 10 languages and a loose reading let each scorer invent commands.
findings.change: Added the frozen rubric_verification_recipes block: one command line per language per probe family, with _general_rules covering the uniform offline build, virtual-machine targets and P3, profiler admissibility, and languages with no separate build step. Cells where no admissible command exists say 'none - ... unsatisfied by construction' NOW, with the reason, as a falsifiable pre-registered claim rather than a scoring-time discovery. global_rules.host_verification.build_recipes now points at this table and at the Diagnostics frozen_diagnostic_configuration as the only two authorised departures from environment.json's recipes, and both are listed in prohibited_at_scoring_time.
findings.quidra_score_direction: LOWER. Quidra has six 'none' cells (no test subcommand, no coverage, no machine-readable test output, no library emission, no binding generator, no cross-target flag), which are now recorded as unsatisfied-by-construction instead of being lost in a rule that would have zeroed every language equally.

findings.defect: Ecosystem Breadth deferred its most outcome-determining input - the per-domain search keywords - to collection time, and evidence was collected in the fixed column order in which Quidra is column 1, so the keyword list would have been written while looking at Quidra's standard library.
findings.change: Added frozen_query_list with the twelve exact query strings (one per domain B01-B12), plus query_exactness, the default sort order, the byte-wise ASCII tie-break, and a no_second_query rule. Added global_rules.evidence_collection_order, which collects evidence in an order ending with Quidra LAST, and added 'altering global_rules.evidence_collection_order, or collecting Quidra's evidence before another language's' to prohibited_at_scoring_time.
findings.quidra_score_direction: LOWER or UNCHANGED. It removes a channel through which the keyword list could have been tuned to Quidra's stdlib coverage; it cannot raise Quidra's N.

findings.defect: 'a maintainer of a major implementation of that language' was load-bearing in E5, I1, I4, I6, Q6 and the Library Availability qualification clause (iii), and was nowhere defined - exactly the holistic judgement this document claims to have eliminated.
findings.change: Added a frozen major_implementations array to every language's entry in official_project_table, with a stated, uniformly applied selection rule (separately developed compiler or interpreter for the same language, a publicly retrievable release within 24 months of the cutoff, acknowledged by the language's official documentation or a recognised standards body). Every occurrence of the undefined phrase - in E5, I1, I4, I6, Q6 and Library Availability clause (iii) - now reads 'an implementation listed in that language's major_implementations', and expanding, narrowing or reinterpreting those lists is in prohibited_at_scoring_time.
findings.quidra_score_direction: LOWER. Quidra's list contains only its reference implementation, while Java gains Eclipse ecj, C++ gains GCC and MSVC, Python gains PyPy and Go gains gccgo, so competitors' IDE, debugger and library-index indicators are decided in their favour by a frozen list instead of by a scorer's judgement.

findings.defect: The Concurrency metric prejudged a competitor's result: CONC-1 admitted 'first-party parallelism' while the metric's na_policy asserted as settled fact that a runtime-level restriction on parallel execution causes C1 to be unsatisfied, so Python's Concurrency score depended on which sentence the scorer read first.
findings.change: CONC-1 now carries an explicit worker_model: a worker may be an OS thread, a process, a lightweight thread, or any other parallelism mechanism provided by the language or its first-party standard library; shared address space is NOT required; the mechanism used is recorded per language. The prejudging clause was deleted from na_policy and replaced with 'C1 is satisfied or not by the measured wall-clock ratio; no language is presumed to pass or fail it, and no runtime property is treated as settling the outcome before measurement.'
findings.quidra_score_direction: LOWER. It removes an assumed failure for a competitor on an indicator Quidra was not assumed to fail.

findings.defect: Readability R3-R6 were not mechanically determined: the measurement script did not exist, the per-language lexing and block-construct tables were deferred to the evidence record, R4/R6 flipped on a single outlier routine, and R1 partly determines R3 by construction because formatters enforce line-length limits.
findings.change: Froze the per-language lexing table (file extensions, comment syntax, string and character literal syntax, block model, routine-header and exclusion regexes) inside the metric; froze the nesting_depth and routine_extent operationalisation so no per-language grammar list has to be assembled at scoring time; changed R4 and R6 from 'no routine exceeds N' to median-and-p95 statistics robust to one outlier; WROTE the reference implementation at scripts/readability_proxy.py, which reads its per-language table from this document rather than carrying one of its own, and recorded its SHA-256 (bcd656da838395ed4de5fcd1cdc5cb31fa448fd21208922a3dbaf74f8df7f16f) together with an integrity rule that stops scoring on a mismatch and re-measures every language if the script is ever corrected. Retired R5 (sigil density) from scoring - measuring its definition over ~690 KB of existing C++ (0.188) and existing Quidra sources (0.171) showed both far below the 0.30 threshold, so it is very likely satisfied by all 10 and carries no information; it is still measured and published. It was NOT re-thresholded, because any tighter threshold could only have been calibrated against values measured from this run's corpora, which spec 32 forbids. The R1/R3 correlation is disclosed in proxy_limitations rather than removed, because deleting R1 would delete a real first-party-artefact property. Also disclosed, on self-review, that the indentation block model reads about one level deeper than the braces model for the same control flow, which makes R4 marginally harder for the two indentation-model languages, Quidra and Python; this is disclosed and not corrected, because correcting it would raise the measured score of the language under evaluation and the offset was not among the audit findings.
findings.quidra_score_direction: MIXED, expected net NEUTRAL to LOWER. Retiring R5 is score-neutral if, as the pre-freeze measurement indicates, all 10 satisfy it. The p95 statistics and the disclosed indentation offset apply identically to every language with the same block model.

findings.defect: Diagnostics measured this document's own flag choice as much as the toolchain: the frozen recipes carried no warning configuration at all, so DIAG-5 produced no diagnostic for several languages on a flag choice rather than on diagnostic quality; and D1 required a column while D2 separately rewarded a caret, leaving 20 points undefined for a toolchain that prints a caret but no numeric column.
findings.change: Added frozen_diagnostic_configuration: one stated principle - use the configuration the language's OWN official documentation presents as the normal development configuration - applied to all 10, with the chosen command and the justifying documentation sentence recorded per language. Added to D1: 'A NUMERIC column or character offset must be printed; a caret or source-excerpt indication alone satisfies D2 but does not satisfy D1.' On self-review, two further defects in the same block were corrected: (i) an optimization_mode_rule, because the inherited performance flags (-O2, -O, -OReleaseFast) would have compared one language's always-on checking against another language's checks-disabled release build on DIAG-8, which is the precise asymmetry spec section 7 warns about - every row now uses that language's own documented default build mode; and (ii) a one_command_rule, because Quidra's row alone listed TWO commands (`quidra check` and `quidra build`), giving one language two chances to emit a diagnostic - the row now names the build command only, and `quidra check --json` is executed separately for D6 alone, exactly as any other language's documented structured-output mode is.
findings.quidra_score_direction: LOWER. Competitors gain the warning and default-build-mode configurations their own documentation prescribes, and Quidra loses a second diagnostic command that no other language had.

findings.defect: indicator_model.unverifiable_rule converted host-provisioning accidents into language scores with no way to tell them apart, and the rule is uniform in wording but not in effect, because Quidra is the one toolchain built from source on this host and so can never fail for a repackaging reason.
findings.change: Added global_rules.tool_availability_states with five distinguishable states (S1 no admissible tool; S2 in the official distribution but absent from this host's repackaged install; S3 admissible but not in the distribution and not installed; S4 blocked by the host OS; S5 present and executed). Tooling's H and Package / Dependency Management's INSTALLED - the two counts that carry the 100-vs-80 step - now count S5 OR S2, so a tool documented as shipping with the official distribution counts as present when it is missing only because of a repackaged install. Every other indicator keeps the conservative rule unchanged. Mandated publication of standard/rubrics/host_limited_indicators.json alongside the Standard results, listing every S2, S3 and S4 case per language, and required it to carry verbatim the disclosure that Quidra's toolchain was built from source here and so cannot fail for a repackaging reason.
findings.quidra_score_direction: LOWER. Rust, Java, Kotlin, C++ and Swift recover H and INSTALLED credit for tools their official distributions ship but this Homebrew/Xcode host does not expose; Quidra gains nothing, because nothing of Quidra's is missing for provisioning reasons.

findings.defect: Portability P6 accepted any 'published language specification/reference standard' with no normativity, conformance or independence test, so self-published markdown in an implementation's own repository scored identically to ISO/IEC 14882 or the Java Language Specification.
findings.change: P6 was split into two equally weighted indicators: P6a (a normative specification that the implementation's own documentation designates as normative AND that contains a conformance statement, OR one published by a standards body independent of the implementation) and P6b (at least two independently developed implementations exist and are acknowledged by official documentation). The level bands were recomputed over 7 indicators and still partition 0-7. Which of the two each language satisfies is recorded. The old id P6 was not reused and no other id was renumbered, so downstream references to P1-P5 still resolve.
findings.quidra_score_direction: LOWER. Quidra's self-published docs/spec are unlikely to satisfy either half, where the single old indicator handed it 20 points; C++, Java and Python are unaffected or gain.

findings.defect: Two of the six Toolchain Stability / Release Maturity indicators measured recent activity rather than maturity and were trivially satisfiable by a weeks-old project: Y1 asked for only 3 tagged releases and Y5 for only 2 releases in 12 months, so a pre-1.0 toolchain could reach 'Developing' (40) on a metric named Release Maturity.
findings.change: Y1 raised from 3 to at least 10 distinct released versions with retrievable release notes, tags or dated download artifacts. Y3 changed from a binary 3-year test to 'at least 10 years elapsed since the first public release'. The discarded 3-year threshold was retained, as the auditor directed, as an age_floor applied BEFORE the indicator count: a toolchain less than 3 years old scores 0 regardless of how many indicators it satisfies. Added an exhaustiveness_verification showing the bands still partition 0-6 satisfied indicators within the group that passes the floor, and 0 for every count within the group that fails it. Y5 was left unchanged: on its own it measures release cadence, which is a real and separately meaningful property, and the auditor's remedy targeted Y1 and Y3.
findings.quidra_score_direction: LOWER, and substantially so. Quidra 0.2.0 fails the raised Y1 and the 10-year Y3, and is very likely caught by the 3-year age floor, which caps it at 0 on this metric. Go, Java, Python, C++, Rust, Swift, Kotlin, TypeScript and Zig are unaffected by the floor.

findings.defect: Dependency Simplicity is very likely non-discriminating under a standard-library-only corpus, and its only live variable - install_units - had an undefined counting rule for exactly the ambiguous cases that decide it (Xcode CLT bundling clang/Swift/XCTest, kotlinc needing a separate JRE, tsc needing node).
findings.change: Froze the counting rule ('a single downloadable distribution providing both compilation and execution of the corpus = 1; a compiler requiring a separately downloaded runtime or SDK = 2') and froze install_units for all 10 languages in install_units_table with a per-language note, plus a correction rule that re-checks every language if one entry proves wrong. Added expected_discrimination_note requiring the near-uniform result to be published with an explicit statement that D_total is expected to be 0 for all 10 and that the remaining spread reflects vendor packaging rather than measured dependency complexity - and disclosing that this is the one Language / Development metric on which a rich library ecosystem can only be a liability, which structurally favours a language that has none.
findings.quidra_score_direction: UNCHANGED for Quidra's own value (install_units 1), but the mandatory disclosure prevents Quidra's high score here being read as a measured ecosystem advantage.

findings.defect: Ecosystem Breadth's domain_satisfaction_rule admitted any 'first-party standard library' library, which would have let environment.json's separately fetched first_party_packages count where the Functionality metric excludes them; and the 12-domain list was asserted neutral rather than derived from anything external, while three of its domains are precisely where the language under evaluation has first-party coverage.
findings.change: domain_satisfaction_rule now defines 'first-party standard library' as a module shipped INSIDE the toolchain distribution under test and nothing else, states that environment.json's first_party_packages do NOT count for any language unless distributed with the toolchain, and routes a separately fetched package published by a language's own project through the package-index clause exactly as a third-party package. Added domain_list_provenance mapping all 12 domains to categories of two external, pre-existing package-index taxonomies (the PyPI trove classifier 'Topic ::' hierarchy and the crates.io category list, both with URL and accession date), drawn from two different language ecosystems so the taxonomy is not taken from any one registry. The domain list itself is unchanged.
findings.quidra_score_direction: LOWER. Quidra's dnn and vision packages are first-party but not shipped with the toolchain, so they can no longer satisfy B04, B05 or B06 by the standard-library route - which was the difference between 20 and 40 on this metric.

findings.defect: With 6 discrete levels across 17 metrics, exact ties are the expected outcome and spec 25.3's unrounded-value rule cannot resolve them, so a tie-break would have been invented after results were visible; and the declared X19/X22 overlap was described as spanning two categories when both metrics are in Language / Development.
findings.change: Added global_rules.tie_handling: languages with identical scores at full precision - on a metric, a category or the Standard Overall Score - are reported at EQUAL RANK under competition ranking (1, 2, 2, 4), no tie-break is applied, and no secondary metric, category, alphabetical order, column order or scorer preference may break one. Added 'breaking a tie between equal scores by any means' to prohibited_at_scoring_time. Corrected overlap_declaration to state that X19's double count falls WITHIN the Language / Development category and to quantify it: concurrency capability contributes to 2 of that category's 8 equally weighted metrics, i.e. 25% of the category rather than 12.5%. The X22/V2 overlap statement was updated to reflect finding 1's widening of V2.
findings.quidra_score_direction: UNCHANGED. A tie rule fixed before any measurement cannot favour a particular language, and the overlap correction changes a disclosure, not a weight.

additional_corrections_from_self_review.defect: A Quidra-specific exemption contradicted a rule stated as neutral elsewhere. The rubric_verification_recipes cell for Quidra's multi_module_build declared that, because quidra 0.2.0 publishes no manifest-driven build subcommand, 'from its declarative manifest' in TEST-2 'does not apply' and V1 would be judged on the other conjunct alone - while global_rules.indicator_model.no_partial_credit requires every conjunct of an AND indicator and no other language was given the same waiver.
additional_corrections_from_self_review.change: The waiver was deleted. V1's text now states both conjuncts explicitly, states that naming a single entry source file that imports the project's other modules is NOT a manifest or project definition, and states that no language is exempted from either conjunct. Quidra's recipe cell now records V1 as unsatisfied by construction for Quidra, with the reason.
